name: Expulsion Science
_comment_group: One more show under the Snapchat heading, cut to Hall of Femme's
design. Everything that makes it a Snapchat pack is Hall of Femme's
and is taken from the same presets rather than restated: the frame
fetch, the 540x960 vertical output, the transcription, the rewrite
that turns speech into report, the stated 40px, the twenty characters
to a line, the freeform text box, the drag.
What makes it a different show is the face and the colours. It is
set in Montserrat Bold, with picked words in Montserrat ExtraBold, in
a purple, a yellow and a black the user pairs between the type and
the card. That is argued below.
The id is kebab-case ASCII because it is also the folder name and the
key everything else refers to; the name is the brand.
_comment_capture: The frame fetch, whole, from content/presets/snapchat-capture.json:
the slider's range, the 540x960 output, the transcription, and the
rewrite that turns it from speech into report. This channel has
nothing to say about any of it that its neighbours do not.
_comment_title: The whole of the difference between this show and Hall of Femme.
Set in Montserrat Bold, with picked words in Montserrat ExtraBold, in
a purple, a yellow or a black the user pairs per frame, on a card.
Everything else - the size, where the lines break, the capitals, the
freeform box, the drag, the margin off the foot of the frame, the
shape of the card - is the Snapchat caption design and is stated once,
in content/presets/snapchat-caption.json.
It used to drop the preset's card and set the caption on the
photograph, in the purple alone, with a dark drop shadow. The show
has since asked for colours for the letters AND for a ground behind
them, which is a request for a card - the panel palette cannot exist
without one (see editor.paletteOf). So it is on the card its carded
siblings use, and what follows from that is written once, in
content/README.md, under 'A channel that set its caption on the
photograph may take the card back'.
Uppercased, inherited, for the reason every pack under this heading
is: at 40px with twenty characters to a line the caption is three
short beats rather than a paragraph, and capitals are what those are
set in. Montserrat has no lower case anybody would call the brand,
and its capitals are geometric enough to carry a line of them.

_comment_color: The show's purple, and the channel's own answer: what every frame
is set in until somebody presses a swatch, since a frame stores no
colour of its own until it is given one (see state.textColorFor).
It opens the list in `colors` below, so the purple swatch is the
one shown as chosen on an untouched frame.
A mid-dark purple had a dark end and a bright end of a photograph
to lose itself in. On a card it is read against a ground somebody
chose instead, which is the whole of why the card it opens on is
_comment_colors: The show's purple, then the yellow and the black it asked for,
offered for the letters and for the card behind them - three
buttons each in the title panel (see editor.renderColorButtons).
The same three in both lists and in one order, which is what Hall
of Femme does and for its reason: the point is the PAIRING. Purple
on yellow is what the show opens on; yellow on black and black on
yellow are a button away. Purple on black is a pairing the list
allows and nobody will keep - the user can see the caption has
`text` reaches the picked words as well as the block until the
highlight row is pressed - see the note on `colors` in
js/channels.js. The highlight here is a WEIGHT and not a colour, so
by default what colour the type is has one answer and not two.
There is no `colors.highlight`: the loader offers the picked words
this same list, for the frame that wants them apart.
_comment_highlight: A picked word is set in Montserrat ExtraBold, in the same colour
as the rest of the block. The highlight here is WEIGHT, exactly
as it is on Hall of Femme: the colour it names is the block's, so
the recolour draws what its neighbours are drawn in and the face
is the whole of the difference. Stated all the same, for the
fallback reason `color` above is stated - a highlight that
changed colour as well as weight would be two highlights.
What is worth being plain about is how much smaller the step is
here than the one it is copied from. Hall of Femme picks out
words at Telegraf 200 against 800, which is a family's two ends
and is as loud as a box; this is 700 against 800, one cut apart
in a text sans, and it is quieter than any other highlight under
this heading. On a card that still reads, because a card is a
controlled ground - which is one more thing the card bought this
show, since over a photograph it was the smallest signal this app
drew.
It is left as the brand asked rather than promoted to a box. The
entry to change, the day this show wants a highlight that carries
at a scroll, is a `fill` beside a `mode` of box - not the face,
which is the part that was specified.
The mode and the scope come from the preset, and the scope is
worth keeping in view: word rather than line, because a caption's
line breaks are wherever the sentence ran out of width, so
picking a LINE out picks out a fragment rather than a thought.
No shadow of its own any more. The drop shadow it used to restate
was there to match the block's on the photograph; with the card
back, the preset's null is right for both (see content/README.md).
_comment_panel: Yellow, and the fill is the one thing about the card this pack
decides: its shape, its padding, its corners and its shadow are
the Snapchat caption design and come from the preset.
Yellow because it is the first colour the show asked for and the
purple reads on it at once. The black card is a button away, under
Taking the card back also moves the words, and by the amount this
pack used to measure: under a line-scope panel the card's padding
is inside the band the rows are stacked by, so the block grows and
the same two-line sentence now stands where Hall of Femme's does,
about twenty pixels higher than it stood on the photograph. The
margin off the foot of the frame is the preset's and unchanged.
